top.line: Agent sessions with one mandate, role and repository can be paused and resumed, so a team's knowledge outlives the team.
top.para: Projects lose their teams, and with them the knowledge needed to fix systems years later, as PHP shows this week. Agent sessions focused on one mandate, role and repository can be paused and picked up again with their conversation, record and code intact. Two PHP-team sessions resumed after 28 hours this week. A newcomer inherits a team, not just code.

in-short.line: Six lines: teams dissolve, fixes get hard, sessions can be frozen, nothing is lost, it happened this week, newcomers inherit a team.
in-short.para: Teams dissolve when projects end or companies are sold, and knowledge leaves with them, so years-later fixes are risky. Agent sessions with one mandate, role and repository can be paused at no cost and resumed with everything intact. Two PHP-team sessions did so after 28 hours. A newcomer inherits the history, the materials and agents ready to change the system.

the-team-that-leaves.line: Every team peaks and then dissolves, and the knowledge goes with the people, until a fix is needed.
the-team-that-leaves.para: A project's sharp team moves on when it dries out, meets its goals or is sold. The know-how, architecture, undocumented reasons and insights leave too. When a fix is needed, as for old PHP now, nobody knows the side effects, and sometimes the pipeline to build and ship the code no longer works.

one-mandate.line: The newsroom and the PHP story run on sessions with one mandate each, which can be paused and resumed.
one-mandate.para: Each agent session does one piece of work with one mandate, role and repository; the PHP story had twenty by 23 October. They keep lessons and debriefs and release their own work. Such a session can be paused at no cost and resumed later with its conversation, reasoning and decisions intact.

this-week.line: Two PHP-team sessions paused on 22 October and resumed 28 hours later by first catching up.
this-week.para: The librarian last committed at 20:20 UTC on 22 October and resumed at 00:12 on 24 October by merging what the team had shipped, then ran its first scheduled pass. The cartographer resumed at 00:16, took in two releases, and was renamed the ontologist. The gap was a day, but the design does not depend on its length.

why-powerful.line: A frozen team can be woken when a fix lands, and a newcomer inherits the history and agents ready to act.
why-powerful.para: Systems went dark this week because their builders had moved on. A frozen team could be woken, read the advisory, know the side effects from its own tests, and propose the change. A new developer inherits the history, materials and agents, and maintenance by the people who know the code becomes cheap enough to sell.

what-it-takes.line: It takes habits: one mandate per session, a written record, a living pipeline, catching up first, keys handed over.
what-it-takes.para: It works because each session has one mandate, writes lessons, debriefs and briefs into the repository, keeps the build and tests running, catches up before acting, and receives keys through a handshake rather than holding secrets indefinitely.

limits.line: The observed gap was 28 hours; context has limits; the platform must keep sessions; people still decide.
limits.para: Months is the design's promise, not yet a measurement. Long sessions summarise their history, so the written record matters. A frozen team depends on the provider keeping the session and on the repository outliving it. Agents keep knowledge within reach; someone still decides.

sources.line: My memo, the PHP site's commits grouped by session, and its team status page.
sources.para: My voice memo of 24 October; the PHP story site's git history from 22 to 24 October, grouped by the Claude Code session in each commit; its team status page; and related articles on agents' records, scheduled agents and maintenance.
